articles.title: East Middleton councillor questions parking charge warning after petrol station breakdown
articles.excerpt: Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned about a parking charge while waiting for the RAC after her car broke down on Oldham Road.
articles.content_html:
Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned she could face a parking charge while waiting for recovery after her car broke down at a petrol station on Oldham Road.

Councillor Jacques, who represents East Middleton on Rochdale Borough Council, described the incident in a public Facebook post, asking whether the business could charge her when her vehicle would not start.

Writing about the breakdown, she said:

“So I’ve broken down in Petrol station on Oldham Road.

“Yes another car that’s absolutely useless ”

She then described a conversation with a member of staff:

“Anyway the guy working there said, I am gunna get charged for parking when his boss comes, as hes saying I can’t stay waiting for RAC!!! I can’t move my car obviously as it won’t start ”

According to her account, the vehicle was beside the station’s tyre inflation equipment. She wrote:

“it’s at the tyre pumper upper so not really blocking anywhere.

“So is this legal does anyone know surly they can’t charge me for breaking down.”

Councillor Jacques said the RAC had given her an estimated arrival window between 9.30pm and 11.30pm.

The screenshot does not establish that a parking charge was subsequently issued, how much was allegedly proposed, or which parking conditions applied. The petrol station is not named in the post, and its account of the conversation is not available.

Could she actually be charged?

A private parking operator can issue a parking charge where it alleges that a driver breached the site’s parking conditions. That is a civil payment demand, rather than a criminal charge. Whether a demand would be enforceable in this particular case cannot be determined from the Facebook post alone. The signage, terms, circumstances of the breakdown and evidence of the recovery arrangements would matter.

However, a breakdown gives a motorist a strong reason to challenge a ticket issued while waiting for repairs or recovery. Citizens Advice specifically identifies being unable to move a broken-down vehicle as grounds for an appeal. That does not guarantee automatic cancellation, but it means a demand should not simply be assumed valid.

Independent parking appeals service POPLA also identifies evidence of a breakdown and a recovery callout as relevant when exceptional circumstances prevented a driver from complying with parking conditions.

Drivers in this situation should retain recovery booking messages, attendance records and photographs of the parking signs. The Competition and Markets Authority advises motorists to preserve evidence when a breakdown occurs and to challenge a disputed charge rather than ignore it.

For now, Councillor Jacques’s post establishes that she reported being warned about a possible charge. It does not establish that she received one or that any payment was legally owed.

Sources: Facebook post attributed to Councillor Georgina Jacques, screenshot supplied to Rochdale Daily; council profile: https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7226; Citizens Advice: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/law-and-courts/parking-tickets/when-to-appeal-a-parking-ticket/; POPLA: https://www.popla.co.uk/appeal-guide; CMA: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/parking-charges-cma-takes-action-to-drive-improvements-for-motorists

We hope Councillor Jacques is rescued promptly and back to her council duties in the morning—with her car feeling rather more cooperative.

articles.title: Holtwood Green’s 56 homes include eight announced First Homes in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Duchy Homes’ Holtwood Green scheme comprises 56 homes on Manchester Old Road. The developer announced eight homes under the First Homes scheme, approximately 14.3% of the total, alongside a three- to five-bedroom market offer.
articles.content_html:
Duchy Homes’ Holtwood Green scheme comprises 56 homes on Manchester Old Road. The developer announced eight homes under the First Homes scheme, approximately 14.3% of the total, alongside a three- to five-bedroom market offer.

The live sales page reviewed advertises prices from £340,995 for a three-bedroom house, with larger properties priced higher. That opening market price should not be described as the price of the discounted First Homes. The eligible plots and their valuations need a separate schedule.

Discounted ownership gives some households a route to buy, but does not answer demand for social rent. Future purchasers also need mortgage eligibility, clear resale conditions and information on charges.

The council’s June 2026 update records construction. School places, healthcare capacity, drainage and transport obligations were not established from the material reviewed. Marketing claims about connectivity are useful context rather than an independent infrastructure assessment.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against Duchy was established. That does not certify the company’s entire legal history or replace scrutiny of warranties and aftercare.

The development contributes to the borough’s housing supply through actual completions. Its full 56 homes should not be treated as still outstanding if some are already occupied.

Location: Manchester Old Road, Middleton

Planning stage: Under construction according to June 2026 council update; homes marketed

Homes: 56 total; eight First Homes announced

Let or for sale: Market sale and discounted First Homes; no social-rent provision verified

Land: Greenfield/brownfield and Green Belt classification not verified

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: The developer’s northwest sales page advertises three-bedroom market homes from £340,995. Different developer URL versions show different plot ranges; these are snapshots, not a final valuation schedule. Exact prices and discounts for the eight First Homes, plus service/estate charges, are not established from the reviewed official records.

Affordable breakdown: Eight First Homes announced out of 56 (about 14.3%); remaining 48 are the market balance on that announced mix. No social-rent provision verified.

Funded school capacity: No scheme-specific funded additional school places, named capital project and opening date were established from the accessible official records reviewed.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: No complete scheme-specific transport funding schedule or evidence of delivered service capacity was established from the accessible official records reviewed. Highway conditions and marketing descriptions do not establish funded bus or rail services.

articles.title: Parkfield House redevelopment brings 20 homes and an 80-bed care home to Middleton
articles.excerpt: Muller Property Group says it has secured approval for 20 townhouses and an 80-bed care home at the former Parkfield House site off Manchester Old Road. The scheme reuses a three-acre brownfield site and involves demolition of the former Chubb Locks headquarters.
articles.content_html:
Muller Property Group says it has secured approval for 20 townhouses and an 80-bed care home at the former Parkfield House site off Manchester Old Road. The scheme reuses a three-acre brownfield site and involves demolition of the former Chubb Locks headquarters.

The building is identified as a non-designated heritage asset. That creates a local heritage issue, but is not the same as demolishing a nationally listed building. The planning decision should explain how the loss was balanced against the public benefits.

The townhouses are described as two- to four-bedroom properties. A secured affordable allocation, sale/rental split and current price list have not been verified. Care accommodation is a different housing product, with fees and support arrangements that should be explained separately.

Eighty care-home beds cannot simply be added to twenty houses and advertised as one hundred ordinary family homes. Any contribution to the housing-delivery measure must use the applicable treatment of communal accommodation.

Access, staff and visitor travel, drainage and the relationship with nearby services are central infrastructure questions. No site-specific capacity assessment was verified here. The developer’s approval statement does not supply that evidence.

No verified adverse builder finding relating to this Middleton scheme was established. A planning dispute elsewhere, or a similarly named company, would not alone establish a problem with this development.

Location: Manchester Old Road, Middleton

Planning stage: Developer reports detailed planning approval; reference 23/00335/FUL

Homes: 20 townhouses; 80 care-home beds reported separately

Let or for sale: Townhouse sale/rental and affordable split unknown; care fees unconfirmed

Land: Three-acre brownfield former headquarters site

Final planning agreement: Muller reports detailed approval, reference 23/00335/FUL. The complete executed deed, conditions and any variations were not verified.

Exact rents / prices: Exact townhouse prices/rents, estate charges and care-home fees have not been established from the reviewed official records or project announcement.

Affordable breakdown: 20 townhouses; no secured affordable count or tenure breakdown verified. The 80 care beds are a separate product and not 80 ordinary family homes.

Funded school capacity: No scheme-specific funded additional school places, named capital project and opening date were established from the accessible official records reviewed.

Funded healthcare capacity: A proposed care home is not evidence of funded GP or NHS capacity. Operator arrangements, NHS commissioning and any extra primary-care capacity were not established.

Funded transport capacity: No complete scheme-specific transport funding schedule or evidence of delivered service capacity was established from the accessible official records reviewed. Highway conditions and marketing descriptions do not establish funded bus or rail services.

articles.title: Simister and Bowlee’s cross-border plan includes 200 homes in Rochdale, not 1,550
articles.excerpt: Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.
articles.content_html:
Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.

The development framework includes a new primary school in the Bury portion, a local centre, a spine road, off-site highway works, active-travel routes, green infrastructure and drainage measures. These are requirements and ambitions for a future neighbourhood, rather than proof that all funding and construction contracts are in place.

Bury’s website cites its own affordable policy rate and an approximate affordable total for the Bury homes. That percentage should not be automatically applied to the Rochdale share. The eventual cross-boundary applications need clear tenure schedules and allocation arrangements.

Residents campaigning against the development raise traffic and drainage concerns. Those are attributed concerns, not verified findings that infrastructure cannot accommodate the plan. The published assessments and conditions must show how risks are addressed.

A specific Rochdale housebuilder and site-specific adverse legal finding have not been verified here. The employment-led Northern Gateway and residential Simister/Bowlee programme should also be kept distinct when explaining approvals.

The core accountability question is whether cross-border delivery provides the services residents actually use, with an enforceable timetable rather than separate promises by different authorities.

Location: Bowlee / Middleton and neighbouring Simister in Bury

Planning stage: Strategic allocation; June 2026 development framework guides later applications

Homes: 1,550 across both boroughs; 200 in Rochdale and 1,350 in Bury

Let or for sale: Affordable housing required; Rochdale-specific number and tenure not established

Land: Largely agricultural land in a former Green Belt allocation

Final planning agreement: Framework/allocation evidence: no executed cross-border development agreement for a detailed housing scheme established.

Exact rents / prices: No exact future rent, sale price, service charge or estate-charge schedule was established from the council/government material reviewed; no reliable scheme-specific current quotation was identified.

Affordable breakdown: 200 of the 1,550 homes are in Rochdale. The Bury affordable percentage must not be applied automatically to those 200; Rochdale-specific signed tenure counts are not established.

Funded school capacity: The framework includes a primary school in Bury. No construction budget, funding agreement, opening date or guaranteed Rochdale pupil access established in the reviewed framework.

Funded healthcare capacity: NHS Greater Manchester’s 1 September 2026 response says it is working with five of six nearby GP practices on estates solutions for existing capacity constraints. NHS Property Services is undertaking capacity assessments. The response provides no funded expansion budget, extra appointment/staffing figures or delivery date.

Funded transport capacity: A spine road, off-site works and active-travel routes are planned. No executed scheme-wide funding/delivery schedule or funded increase in bus capacity established.

articles.title: Stakehill’s revised 1,300-home proposal raises questions over affordability and transport
articles.excerpt: Barratt is preparing a revised neighbourhood at Stakehill with around 1,300 homes. Its consultation proposes 15% affordable housing: approximately 195 homes if the final total remains 1,300. The remaining tenure detail and actual prices have not been established.
articles.content_html:
Barratt is preparing a revised neighbourhood at Stakehill with around 1,300 homes. Its consultation proposes 15% affordable housing: approximately 195 homes if the final total remains 1,300. The remaining tenure detail and actual prices have not been established.

This is part of, rather than additional to, the wider Stakehill allocation. The earlier Redrow application sought 233 detailed-consent homes and up to 1,147 outline homes. Those figures describe an earlier version and must not be added to the revised proposal.

Barratt describes an 88-hectare site of mainly agricultural fields. School expansion and a possible Slattocks station feature in the wider planning ambitions. A station proposal is not an operating service or a confirmed opening date. The decisive evidence will be funded transport measures, school capacity and occupation triggers.

Barratt Redrow joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

The scheme could make a substantial contribution to housing supply over several years. Whether it meets local needs depends on who can afford the homes and how quickly the supporting services arrive.

Location: Stakehill / Thornham / Slattocks

Planning stage: Revised application intended for autumn 2026; current submission status needs confirmation

Homes: About 1,300 in Barratt’s proposal; around 1,680 across the wider allocation

Let or for sale: Proposed 15% affordable; detailed rental/ownership split and prices unconfirmed

Land: Predominantly agricultural greenfield; allocation includes land released from Green Belt

Final planning agreement: Revised proposal: no executed agreement for this version verified. A consultation percentage is not a signed affordable-housing obligation.

Exact rents / prices: No exact future rent, sale price, service charge or estate-charge schedule was established from the council/government material reviewed; no reliable scheme-specific current quotation was identified.

Affordable breakdown: 15% proposed: approximately 195 of 1,300 if those figures survive approval. Social rent, other rent, shared ownership and discounted-sale counts are not disclosed in the reviewed proposal.

Funded school capacity: School expansion is envisaged, but a funded project, additional places and occupation-linked opening date were not verified.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: The council capital programme includes rail-corridor development work and Slattocks feasibility/masterplanning. A full new-station construction budget, operator commitment and opening date were not established.

articles.title: Man Injured in Altercation on Rochdale Road, Middleton
articles.excerpt: A man sustained injuries during an altercation on Rochdale Road in Middleton on October 11, prompting a response from police and ambulances shortly after the incident.
articles.content_html:
A man was injured during an altercation on Rochdale Road in Middleton on the afternoon of October 11. Greater Manchester Police received reports of a disturbance at approximately 4:30pm and dispatched several police cars and two ambulances to the scene.

Upon arrival, officers located the injured man, whose injuries are not believed to be life-threatening. The exact circumstances surrounding the incident remain unclear as investigations are ongoing, according to a police statement.

The police confirmed that they are working to determine the full details of the incident. No further information regarding potential suspects or the nature of the altercation has been released.

Local residents may notice an increased police presence on Rochdale Road as inquiries continue. Anyone with information about the incident is encouraged to contact the authorities.

articles.title: Brandlehow Drive, roadworks in Middleton on 12 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council lists work affecting Brandlehow Drive in Middleton; expected timings: 8.30am–4pm on Monday, 12 October 2026.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has published a traffic notice for Brandlehow Drive in Middleton. The council lists the expected start and finish as 8.30am–4pm on Monday, 12 October 2026.

The council gives the reason as To carry out maintenance on the substation. The notice describes the affected area as follows: The part of Brandlehow Drive between the junctions of Latrigg Crescent and Lingholme Drive will be temporarily closed.

The published alternative route is Latrigg Crescent, Windermere Road and Brandlehow Drive. These are the details in the council's current published record, rather than confirmation that work has started or finished. Readers travelling through the area can check the original Rochdale Borough Council notice for any subsequent amendments.

articles.title: High Court Rules Against Filmmaker in Hopwood Hall Restoration Dispute
articles.excerpt: A recent High Court ruling has concluded a legal battle between American filmmaker Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council over the future of Hopwood Hall in Middleton.
articles.content_html:
A High Court ruling has determined that American filmmaker Hopwood DePree does not have the right to purchase Hopwood Hall, a Grade-II* listed building in Middleton, following a protracted legal dispute with Rochdale Council. The decision was announced during a hearing at the Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, marking a significant setback for DePree, who has invested over £750,000 in efforts to restore the historic estate.

The saga began in 2017 when DePree signed an options agreement with the council to lead the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall. His vision included transforming the 1400s stately home into a wedding and hospitality venue, complete with a hotel retreat, gift shop, and guided tours. DePree engaged the local community in his restoration efforts, which included extensive work on the hall's gardens and interior.

Before DePree's involvement, Hopwood Hall had fallen into disrepair, with its last known use being as part of De La Salle College, which closed in 1989. The hall had previously served as a venue for various events, including an underground bar and nightclub during the 1960s and 70s, where notable acts such as Black Sabbath performed.

The ruling concludes a decade-long effort by DePree to revive the hall, which has been under the ownership of Rochdale Council since the college's closure. The future of Hopwood Hall now remains uncertain as the council considers its next steps regarding the estate.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The Hopwood Hall saga | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The Hopwood Hall saga George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 10, 2026 | 8:44 AM Print The Grade-II listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton When an American filmmaker and Rochdale council signed an agreement over a shared ambition to restore Hopwood Hall, no one could have fathomed the furious saga that unfolded. What started as a harmonious relationship between Hopwood DePree and the local authority ended up with them being on opposite sides of a court room. Mr DePree claims ancestral connections to the Grade-II* listed building in Middleton. His dream was to bring the 1400s stately home back to life. He even roped in the local community to help him do it, apparently spending more than £750,000 on the project. On what he described as a ‘sad day’ in Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, his dream was crushed. The High Court ruled in favour of the council following a legal battle over whether Mr DePree had the right to buy the estate or not. The saga began in 2017 when Hopwood DePree signed an options agreement with town hall bosses to lead the redevelopment of the hall. Since then he has led a decade-long community effort to do exactly that. The Hollywood man’s vision saw the hall transformed into a wedding and hospitality venue, with a hotel ‘retreat’, gift shop and guided tours all part of the package. His team could regularly be seen working on the hall’s gardens and titivating the interior in the years since. Before Mr DePree came along, the hall had fallen into disrepair and irrelevance. Its last known use was as part of the De La Salle College, which shut down in 1989. During the 1960s and 70s it was said to be the setting for an underground bar and nightclub. It is believed that Ozzy Osbourne’s band Black Sabbath and other iconic performers played there. Since the closure of the college, the hall has been in the possession of Rochdale council. The American even created a Youtube series and wrote a book about his journey refurbishing what he affectionately called ‘Downton Shabby’. However, this journey came to an abrupt halt when the council ended the agreement in October 2024 and, without warning, barred Mr DePree and his group from the building. Part of the options agreement allowed the US actor and producer to purchase the historic asset from landowners Rochdale council for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. Mr DePree attempted to exercise that option the day before the council ended the agreement, which was denied by town hall chiefs. Since then, a two-year-long war of words has raged between Mr DePree and Rochdale council. The American threatened legal action for months, but the council never budged. Mr DePree believed the local authority acted unlawfully by denying his ‘legally binding’ option to buy Hopwood Hall. At the time, the council said they ended the agreement because Mr DePree hadn’t made enough progress with the restoration effort. This expulsion from the estate came following a number of extensions to the agreement made by the council. The local authority even granted ‘change of use’ planning permission to Mr DePree for Hopwood Hall in 2022. Until the two sides decided to settle the matter in High Court, it was unclear just how important that planning permission was. Effectively, approved planning permission was the trigger to open up the option for Mr DePree to have the estate transferred to him. The High Court played host to Hopwood Hall Estate Ltd vs Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council this week. In the words of Mr DePree’s barrister, Ashley Bowes, the planning permission was ‘the star of the show’. The court heard details of the dispute over whether Mr DePree had authority to trigger the transfer of the property based on the approved plans. The council’s barrister Geraint Wheatley said the plans did not go far enough in demonstrating a serious commitment to reinstate and refurbish the 1400s building, as required by the options agreement. He described the ‘ruined’ hall as needing far more than some internal works to bring it back to a state of habitation. According to Mr Wheatley the conditions of the options agreement to trigger the purchase of the hall had four elements – authorisation to reinstate and refurbish the building; agreed standard of refurbishment between the parties (fit for habitation); English Heritage approval; and that the property would be reinstated and refurbished in whole, not in part. The defence barrister pointed out that getting permission for events and hospitality space for part of the ground floor doesn’t relate to the building ‘in whole’, as requested in the agreement clause. He also pointed out that the plans wouldn’t have seen the hall be fit for habitation or reinstated and refurbished. “Obtaining a mere ‘change of use’ permission doesn’t show a great deal of commitment,” Mr Wheatley told the court. “Plans of physical work show that commitment.” Mr Wheatley also tried to argue that English Heritage approval wasn’t given. But His Honour Judge Hodge KC believed the organisation’s support for the 2022 plans qualified as their approval. Buoyed by the judge agreeing with one point of the claimant, Dr Bowes said the 2022 application was internal work that would have created an events and hospitality space and enabled future work to be reinstated and refurbished. He said the claimant didn’t think anything more than a change of use application would be necessary to trigger the purchase as it wasn’t specified in the agreement. Dr Bowes said it was ‘wishful thinking’ on the council’s part that a community group would spend huge sums of money drawing up plans for physical works when they didn’t think it would be necessary. After delving into detailed planning legislation; the interpretation of wording in the agreement; and the cross-examinations of both Hopwood DePree and council boss for economy and place, Mark Robinson, the judge ruled in favour of the defendant – Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council. His Honour Judge Hodge KC described how the planning application did not cover the whole of the property or showcase the ability to reinstate and refurbish Hopwood Hall, as required in the options agreement. He added: “I am satisfied, for the reasons I have given, that the planning permission does not satisfy the requirements of the options agreement. I therefore refuse to grant the relief sought by the claimant.” A lengthy saga was ended by a two-day trial. Instead of getting Hopwood Hall for £1, Mr DePree was landed with a £114,000 bill to cover the council’s court costs. However, the American said the fight isn’t over and Hopwood Hall ‘must be saved’. He didn’t confirm whether his team would appeal the judgement, but they have until November 18 to do so. Speaking after the case, Mr DePree said: “Obviously I am incredibly disappointed. Not just me but the community of support around the world and the UK charitable groups as well. “I am already discussing with my legal team about the next steps. In the meantime I hope Rochdale council will be watching over Hopwood Hall because we will be keeping an eye on them. “We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved. In the two years we have been locked out the gardens have gone into wrack and ruin. I hope they will step up and save the hall. I still think the community group and I are the best people to take this forward. “I am getting messages from around the world with people offering money and support. It is a sad day but we will have to have a look at our options.” The town hall has committed to maintaining the building and have commissioned a feasibility study to look into possible future uses for the historic asset. A Rochdale council spokesperson said: “We are pleased with today’s judgement. It’s a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself. “We’re now focussed on moving forward. More than £1.6m has been spent on the hall by ourselves and Historic England since 2017 and we will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall’s long-term future will be considered in due course. “One thing we are clear on is, whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us? articles.title: £12m plan aims to bring Storage World Middleton site back to life after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: A £12m rebirth bid has been launched for the Storage World site in Middleton, more than a year after a devastating fire destroyed the Old Hall Street facility.
articles.content_html:
A £12m bid to bring the Storage World site in Middleton back to life has been launched, marking a major potential investment in an important part of the town centre following last year's devastating fire.

The proposals concern the Storage World site on Old Hall Street, next to Middleton Arena. The former storage facility was badly damaged by a major blaze in June 2025, which burned for several days and led to demolition of the building. No injuries were reported, although customers and businesses suffered significant losses.

Place North West has reported that Storage World has now launched a £12m rebirth bid for the site. The move comes as regeneration work and planning for the wider Middleton town centre area continues.

Official Rochdale Development Agency updates show that the council and RDA have remained in discussions with Storage World since the fire. In June, the RDA said it was working with stakeholders to develop key principles for the area, including the potential to deliver improvements to Middleton Arena and create a new public space. It also confirmed that discussions with Storage World were continuing with input from Rochdale Borough Council's planning team.

The site is particularly significant because of its position beside Middleton Arena and within an area being considered as part of wider plans for the future of Middleton town centre. Earlier council reports said the outcomes of discussions over Storage World and the arena would feed into wider masterplanning work.

Before the fire, Storage World operated a large self-storage and workspace facility from Old Hall Street. The Middleton operation had previously expanded as demand grew, with the company providing traditional storage alongside space used by small and online businesses.

The 2025 blaze had a substantial impact on customers. Fire crews worked for days at the scene and parts of the building were demolished while firefighting operations were still under way to allow crews safe access. Storage World said at the time that its team was devastated by the impact on customers and the wider community.

The latest £12m proposal therefore represents a potentially significant next chapter for a prominent town-centre site and comes at a time when Middleton is the subject of wider regeneration and masterplanning proposals.

Rochdale Daily will update this story as further planning documents and details of the proposed redevelopment become publicly available.

articles.title: Middleton protest planned as organiser sets out bail conditions ahead of event
articles.excerpt: A protest is planned in Middleton Gardens on 8 August, with organiser Jamie Thomason outlining his intended arrangements and referring to bail conditions while police are expected to oversee the event.
articles.content_html:
A public protest is due to take place in Middleton Gardens on Saturday, 8 August, with organiser Jamie Thomason stating he intends to comply with his bail conditions while addressing supporters before leaving the area. According to a statement published on social media, Greater Manchester Police will have officers present during the event, with police liaison officers said to be aware of the arrangements.

In his announcement, Thomason said he would be joined by several guest speakers from across the UK, including Ashlea Simon of All for England, Dorothy Jones and Pag Billy UK, with additional speakers yet to be confirmed. He described his planned speech as being based on information which he says can be verified through publicly available sources and encouraged supporters to attend the demonstration.

Thomason also referred to his current bail conditions, stating that he is prohibited from congregating with more than ten people. He asked supporters not to approach him in groups, saying he had agreed with Greater Manchester Police that he would attend, deliver his speech and leave Middleton immediately afterwards. He also stated that he would give his speech from a distance and would not become involved in any confrontation because he did not intend to breach his bail conditions.

Rochdale Daily has not independently verified the specific bail conditions referred to in Thomason's post, and reports them only as claims made by the organiser himself.

The right to peaceful protest is protected in UK law under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, although that right is subject to restrictions where they are lawful, necessary and proportionate. Police have powers under the Public Order Act 1986, as amended by more recent legislation including the Public Order Act 2023, to impose conditions on public assemblies where they reasonably believe serious public disorder, serious disruption, intimidation or damage may occur. Participants are expected to comply with any lawful conditions imposed.

Greater Manchester Police has previously stated that its role at public demonstrations is to facilitate peaceful and lawful protest while taking action where criminal offences are committed or where public safety is at risk. Depending on the circumstances, officers may deploy protest liaison teams, public order officers or other resources to manage events and minimise disruption to the wider community.

The planned demonstration is likely to attract differing opinions from residents. Supporters say the event is intended to raise awareness of issues they believe are affecting communities across the country, while others are expected to disagree with both the organisers and the views expressed. Peaceful disagreement and lawful protest are protected rights, provided they remain within the limits of the law.

Anyone travelling through Middleton town centre on Saturday should be aware that there may be an increased police presence around Middleton Gardens while the demonstration takes place. At the time of publication, no official road closures, dispersal orders or protest conditions had been publicly announced.

Rochdale Daily has contacted Greater Manchester Police for comment to confirm the policing arrangements for the event, including whether officers will be deployed, whether any conditions have been imposed under public order legislation, and whether any road closures, dispersal powers or other measures are anticipated. This article will be updated if and when a response is received.
